titleStmt.title: The Developmental Theory of the Gender Gap: Women’s and Men’s Voting Behavior in Global Perspective
titleStmt.author: Ronald Inglehart
Pippa Norris

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: The Developmental Theory of the Gender Gap: Women’s and Men’s Voting Behavior in Global Perspective

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: mechanism
span.quote: Our argument is based on a developmental theory of the gender gap suggesting that long-term structural and cultural trends, which have transformed women’s and men’s lives, have gradually produced realignment in gender politics in postindustrial societies.

span.label: gender gap in voting
span.quote: The analysis demonstrates that gender differences in voting behavior have been realigning in postindustrial societies.

span.label: observational-study
span.quote: For data we draw on the World Values Surveys (WVS), carried out in three waves in the early 1980s, the early 1990s, and the mid-1990s.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Modernization converges men's and women's roles through the paid labour market, education and changed family structure, which in turn changes their political preferences
span.quote: In postindustrial societies gender roles have increasingly converged due to a structural revolution in the paid labor force, in educational opportunities for women, and in the characteristics of modern families.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Value change — the spread of postmaterialist and egalitarian/feminist attitudes — pulls women's vote leftwards
span.quote: That is, women in advanced industrialized societies are shifting left because of a broad process of value changes, particularly the shift towards more egalitarian attitudes associated with postmaterialism and feminism.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Generational turnover: as younger cohorts replace older ones the aggregate gap keeps moving left
span.quote: If this is a generational rather than a life-cycle effect, as seems most likely, it suggests that the process of generational turnover will probably continue to move women leftwards.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Occupational segregation concentrates working women in low-paid and public-sector jobs, encouraging support for parties of the left
span.quote: Women’s support for parties of the left may be encouraged by pervasive patterns of horizontal and vertical occupational segregation.

span.label: The survey data do not cover consistent over-time trends for most of the countries compared, so the wider comparison is cross-sectional (1990s only).
span.note: what this limits: the cross-national comparison: WE LACK EVIDENCE IN THE WORLD VALUES SURVEY FOR CONSISTENT TRENDS OVER TIME IN A WIDER RANGE OF SOCIETIES
span.quote: We lack evidence in the World Values Survey for consistent trends over time in a wider range of societies but we can compare the size and direction of the voting gap in the 1990s in the 36 countries shown in Table 3 and Figure 2.

span.label: No systematic comparative evidence exists before the 1980s, so long-term secular change has to be inferred from age-cohort differences rather than observed directly.
span.note: what this limits: the long-term secular claim: WE LACK SYSTEMATIC COMPARATIVE EVIDENCE ... FROM THE ERA PRIOR TO THE 1980S, so it is inferred rather than observed
span.quote: Although we lack systematic comparative evidence in the World Values Survey from the era prior to the 1980s, we would expect to find long-term secular trends reflected in differences between the respective age cohorts, with the younger cohort of women most strongly influenced by the transformation of sex roles in advanced industrial societies.

span.label: The analysis covers only one dimension of a multidimensional phenomenon: vote choice, not partisanship, attitudes, or civic engagement.
span.note: what this limits: every use of the phrase gender gap drawn from this work: THE TERM ... CONCERNS A MULTIDIMENSIONAL POLITICAL PHENOMENON, and only vote choice is measured here
span.quote: We recognize that the term “gender gap” concerns a multidimensional political phenomenon that can refer to any political differences between women and men, such as in their voting behavior, partisanship, attitudes and opinions, or civic engagement, at mass or elite levels, but the concern of this article is restricted to comparing voting choices.

span.label: The realignment is uneven across countries and may reflect country-specific circumstances the theory does not model.
span.note: what this limits: the generality of the realignment claim: THE PROCESS IS FAR FROM UNIFORM, PROBABLY REFLECTING PARTICULAR CIRCUMSTANCES WITHIN EACH COUNTRY
span.quote: It should be stressed that the process is far from uniform, probably reflecting particular circumstances within each country, such as the pattern of party competition, the predominant issue agenda, and the strength of the organized women’s movement.

span.label: The headline realignment is explicitly not global, although the title says global perspective: the old pattern is reported as persisting in postcommunist and developing societies.
span.note: what this limits: the claim that women have realigned to the left worldwide: the paper reports the modern gap in postindustrial and some West European states, and states it was not yet evident in postcommunist or developing societies
span.quote: The modern gender gap is not confined to the United States, as particularistic accounts suggest, but is also evident by the 1990s in some West European states. Nevertheless this pattern was not yet evident in postcommunist societies or developing societies

span.label: Sympathy for feminist ideals is measured by two proxies chosen as indicators, so the construct is interpretive rather than observed.
span.note: what this limits: the feminism controls in this analysis: they are confidence in the women's movement and attitudes towards abortion, described as key indicators of sympathy for feminist ideals rather than direct measures of it
span.quote: the size of the gender gap controlling for the effects of confidence in the women’s movement and also attitudes towards abortion, understood as key indicators of sympathy for feminist ideals

span.label: structural controls were introduced and the gender gap re-estimated in each country
span.note: eliminates: that the modern gender gap is a by-product of structural differences - education, income, labour-force participation - rather than a value shift
span.quote: The modern gender gap was maintained in the United States, France, and Germany after introducing structural controls, but it became insignificant in every country except the United States once we controlled for cultural attitudes.

span.label: traditional gender gap
span.quote: Here, it is examined whether this traditional gender gap persists today, or whether gender cleavages in the electorate have converged

span.label: modern gender gap
span.quote: whether the phenomenon of the modern gender gap, with women more left wing, has become evident elsewhere.

span.label: World Values Surveys
span.quote: The article draws on evidence from the World Values Surveys in the early 1980s, and the early and mid-1990s carried out in over sixty countries around the world.

span.label: gender gap - TRADITIONAL: women voting more conservatively and participating less than men, the orthodoxy the article sets out to test
span.quote: Studies carried out in many countries in previous decades found that women were more conservative than men and less likely to participate in politics.

span.label: gender gap - MODERN: women voting to the LEFT of men, the opposite sign under the same term, reported for postindustrial societies by the 1990s
span.quote: By the 1990s women voters in these nations proved significantly more leftwing than men, even after introducing a range of social controls.

span.label: sympathy for feminist ideals - operationalised as two survey items: confidence in the women's movement and attitudes towards abortion
span.quote: the size of the gender gap controlling for the effects of confidence in the women’s movement and also attitudes towards abortion, understood as key indicators of sympathy for feminist ideals

span.quote: We argue that a developmental theory can be used to explain this phenomenon, in which the transformation of sex roles in postindustrial societies has influenced the process of value change.

span.quote: First, we found that in established democracies as recently as the early 1980s, women tended to be more conservative than men, in their ideology and voting behavior, as earlier studies suggested.

span.label: phenomenon: the gender gap in voting behaviour and its reversal as societies become postindustrial
span.note: a second reading DIFFERING from the recorded value. See Q-1176, Q-1178.
span.quote: As expected we found a different pattern, with the traditional gender gap being prevalent in the 1990s.

span.label: extends → Inglehart (1977) and Norris (1988) predictions that women's relative conservatism would disappear
span.quote: By the 1990s these predictions appear to have been confirmed.

span.label: builds-on → Studlar, McAllister and Hayes (1998)
span.quote: What this suggests, as Studlar, McAllister and Hayes (1998) noted in their comparison of the United States, Australia, and Britain, is that the modern gender gap is more strongly the product of attitudinal rather than structural variables.

span.label: traditional gender gap —contrasted-with→ modern gender gap
span.quote: Here, it is examined whether this traditional gender gap persists today, or whether gender cleavages in the electorate have converged, and whether the phenomenon of the modern gender gap, with women more left wing, has become evident elsewhere.

span.label: ANOVA
span.quote: ANOVA tests the statistical significance of the differences in the group means within each country.

span.label: difference between group means
span.quote: This scale allowed us to compare the mean left–right position of women and men voters within each country, calculating the voting gap as the difference between group means, checked for significance with ANOVA.

span.label: ordinary least squares regression
span.quote: To do this we use ordinary least squared regression models with the 10-point left–right voting scale as the dependent variable.

span.label: standardized regression coefficient
span.quote: on OLS regression analysis. The figures are standardized Beta coefficients representing the impact of the independent variables on the 10-point left–right voting scale. (See Appendix for details.) *p=.05;

span.label: correlation
span.quote: Overall where people placed themselves on the ideological scale was closely associated (r=.46) with their position on the voting scale, increasing confidence in the consistency of this measure.

span.label: By the 1990s women in postindustrial societies voted significantly further to the left than men, and the difference survived a battery of social controls.
span.quote: By the 1990s women voters in these nations proved significantly more leftwing than men, even after introducing a range of social controls.

span.label: The leftward shift did not appear in postcommunist or developing societies, where women were still voting further right than men in the mid-1990s.
span.quote: Nevertheless this pattern was not yet evident in postcommunist societies or developing societies, where the traditional gender gap persists into the mid-1990s with women voters more rightwing than men.

span.label: Averaged by type of society, the voting gap was +.10 (women left) in advanced industrialized democracies, -.08 in postcommunist societies and -.14 in developing societies (women right).
span.quote: Across all advanced industrialized democracies the gender gap in voting was +.10 (with women leaning left), whereas it was –.08 in postcommunist societies, and –.14 in developing societies (with women leaning right).

span.label: In postindustrial societies the modern gender gap survives structural controls but shrinks once cultural attitudes are added to the model.
span.quote: In postindustrial societies the modern gender gap persists even after introducing a range of social controls but the size of the gap diminishes once we take into account cultural factors.

span.label: The gap is therefore attributed mainly to women's and men's differing value orientations — postmaterialism and support for the women's movement — rather than to differences in their lifestyles.
span.quote: This finding suggests that the modern gender gap is more strongly the product of cultural differences between women and men in their value orientations, especially attitudes towards postmaterialism and the women’s movement, rather than differences in their lifestyles.

span.label: Within established democracies the gap reverses across age groups: in the youngest cohort women are far to the left of men, while among the over-65s women are more conservative than men.
span.quote: In established democracies the pattern of the gender gap by age group did prove to be an important indicator of generational change: among the youngest group women are far more left wing than men (see Figure 4) whereas among the over-65s the gender gap reversed, with women more conservative.

span.label: Country by country, the modern gap held up under structural controls in the United States, France and Germany, but only the United States kept a significant gap after cultural attitudes were controlled.
span.quote: The modern gender gap was maintained in the United States, France, and Germany after introducing structural controls, but it became insignificant in every country except the United States once we controlled for cultural attitudes.

span.label: On ideological self-placement in the 1990s, women were significantly more right wing than men in only six of 57 nations, overturning the old orthodoxy of female conservatism.
span.quote: The results confirm that by the 1990s women were significantly more right wing than men in only a few societies (six out of 57 nations).

span.label: In Europe the convergence came from women moving left while men stayed put: the mean male position was essentially unchanged from 1973 to 1999 while the mean female position moved from 5.61 to 5.20.
span.quote: The mean position of women changed from 5.61 in 1973 to 5.20 in 1999.

span.label: The American gender gap is not exceptional in size; larger ideological gaps appear in Germany, the Netherlands and Denmark.
span.quote: Although this phenomenon has received most attention in the United States, it is striking that the size of the ideological gap there is far from exceptional, since even larger gaps are evident in comparable democracies like Germany, the Netherlands, and Denmark.

span.label: traditional gender gap
span.quote: women were found to be more apt than men to support center–right parties in Western Europe and in the United States, a pattern which we can term the traditional gender gap

span.label: modern gender gap
span.quote: During the last decade, however, there has been much speculation, although little concrete evidence, that women were continuing to realign towards the left throughout advanced industrial societies, a situation that we will term the modern gender gap, replicating the pattern evident since the early 1980s in the United States.

span.label: developmental theory of the gender gap
span.term: developmental theory of the gender gap
span.quote: Our argument is based on a developmental theory of the gender gap suggesting that long-term structural and cultural trends, which have transformed women’s and men’s lives, have gradually produced realignment in gender politics in postindustrial societies.

span.label: gender dealignment
span.quote: This orthodoxy came under increasing challenge during the 1980s since scholars in many Western countries emphasized a pattern of gender dealignment in the electorate, or a weakening of women’s traditional conservatism.

span.label: ideological gap
span.quote: The “ideological gap” is calculated as the difference in the mean self-placement of women and men on these scales; for example, if women place themselves at 5.5 and men at 6.8, the resultant ideological gap is estimated at +1.3.

span.label: gender
span.quote: In Model 1 we explore the impact of gender on the left–right voting scale without any controls.

span.label: 10-point left–right voting scale (expert-coded position of the party the respondent would vote for)
span.term: 10-point left–right voting scale (expert-coded position of the party the respondent would vote for)
span.quote: To do this we use ordinary least squared regression models with the 10-point left–right voting scale as the dependent variable.

span.label: structural characteristics: religiosity, labour force participation, education, age, socioeconomic status
span.term: structural characteristics: religiosity, labour force participation, education, age, socioeconomic status
span.quote: Model 2 adds controls for religiosity, labor force participation, education, age and the respondent’s socioeconomic status.

span.label: cultural attitudes: postmaterialist values, support for the women's movement, abortion, role of government
span.term: cultural attitudes: postmaterialist values, support for the women's movement, abortion, role of government
span.quote: Model 3 adds controls for support for postmaterialist values, support for the women’s movement, for abortion and for left–right attitudes toward the role of government in the economy.

span.label: generational cohort
span.quote: Within postindustrial societies we would also predict that the gender gap would reverse by generational cohort, given the way that changes in lifestyles and cultural trends have transformed the lives of older and younger groups of women.

span.label: type of society (postindustrial, postcommunist, developing)
span.quote: This again reinforces the finding that any global analysis of the gender gap needs to take account of the type of society, as well as individual level factors.

span.label: +.10 / –.08 / –.14 — Mean gender gap on the 10-point voting scale in advanced industrialized, postcommunist and developing societies respectively (positive = women further left)
span.quote: Across all advanced industrialized democracies the gender gap in voting was +.10 (with women leaning left), whereas it was –.08 in postcommunist societies, and –.14 in developing societies (with women leaning right).

span.label: r=.46 — Correlation between respondents' left-right ideological self-placement and the expert-coded left-right position of the party they intended to vote for, used as a reliability check on the voting scale
span.quote: Overall where people placed themselves on the ideological scale was closely associated (r=.46) with their position on the voting scale, increasing confidence in the consistency of this measure.

span.label: six out of 57 nations — Number of countries in the 1990s where women were significantly more right wing than men on ideological self-placement
span.quote: The results confirm that by the 1990s women were significantly more right wing than men in only a few societies (six out of 57 nations).

span.label: fourteen countries — Number of countries in the same comparison where women were significantly more left wing than men
span.quote: In most nations women proved largely similar to men, but they were significantly more left wing in fourteen countries.

span.label: sixty societies — Number of societies compared across the three waves of the World Values Surveys
span.quote: In total these surveys allow us to compare sixty societies around the globe, although not all countries were included in each wave.

span.label: 5.61 in 1973 to 5.20 in 1999 — Mean ideological self-placement of European women on the 10-point left-right scale at the start and end of the Eurobarometer series
span.quote: The mean position of women changed from 5.61 in 1973 to 5.20 in 1999.

span.label: six out of ten nations — Number of advanced industrialized countries (of the ten with a complete set of controls) where women voted significantly further left than men in the uncontrolled model
span.quote: The results in Model 1 confirm that by the 1990s among advanced industrialized societies women proved significantly more left wing than men in six out of ten nations, there was no significant difference in three countries, and in one (Finland) women were more right wing.

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1177/0192512100214007.
